name: Tax Form Navigator
tag: Explains IRS forms like the 1099-A and 1099-B in plain language, box by box.

scenarios.title: Read a 1099-B from a broker
scenarios.ask: I sold shares for ${proceeds}. My basis was ${basis} and I held them {holding}. Walk me through the 1099-B.
steps: Found the key boxes: 1a description, 1b date acquired, 1c date sold, 1d proceeds and 1e cost basis.
Held {holding}, so it belongs on the matching short-term or long-term part of Form 8949.
Showed how Form 8949 totals carry to Schedule D.
followups: Gains on assets held more than one year are long-term and usually taxed at lower federal rates than short-term gains, which are taxed like ordinary income.
Some brokers don't report basis for older or transferred shares. You then need your own records of what you paid, and the navigator shows where to enter it.

scenarios.title: Understand a 1099-A after foreclosure
scenarios.ask: I got a 1099-A. The loan balance was ${owed} and the property's fair market value is ${fmv}. What does this mean?
steps: Explained the boxes: 1 date of acquisition, 2 principal balance, 4 fair market value, 5 personal liability, 6 property description.
Balance minus value: ${=max(0, owed - fmv)} of debt above the property's value.
Box 5 marked {recourse}. This changes how the sale amount is figured and whether canceled debt may follow.
Listed what to look for next: a possible 1099-C and your original purchase records.

result.title: Your 1099-A in plain English
rows: Educational guide; talk to a tax professional

followups: No. It reports that the lender took the property. You may have a gain or loss on the disposition, which depends on your basis and the loan terms.

For recourse loans, the amount realized is generally tied to fair market value and any forgiven balance may be canceled debt. For nonrecourse loans, it is generally tied to the full balance. A tax professional should confirm your case.

scenarios.title: Organize all your tax forms
scenarios.ask: I have {forms} tax forms from {payers} different payers. Tell me what each is for and what's missing.
steps: Grouped {forms} sample forms by type: wages, interest, dividends, brokerage and property.
Wrote a two-line summary of each form.
Compared {payers} payers with last year's list and flagged {=max(0, round(payers * 0.2))} likely missing forms.
Built a checklist to share with your tax preparer.
followups: Many 1099 forms are due to recipients by the end of January or mid-February, and corrected forms can come later. Check with each payer if one is missing.
No. It explains forms and builds a checklist. Filing is done by you or your tax preparer.
